name: Bata shoe factory, East Tilbury
text: Your train passes near the old Bata shoe factory, on the train's {side}, founded in 1932 by the Czech shoe maker Tomáš Baťa. Around it grew a company town with modernist buildings, worker housing, schools, a hotel and a theatre; it made shoes for more than 70 years until it closed in 2005.

name: All Saints Church, Vange
text: Your train passes near All Saints Church in Vange, on the train's {side}, thought to date from around 1328 and believed to be the oldest surviving church in Basildon. Its last service was held in 1994, and it has been cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust since 2003.

name: Basildon Town Centre
text: Your train passes near Basildon Town Centre, on the train's {side}, planned for one of England's first new towns after the Second World War. From 1956 a large lit sign beside the railway announced “This is the site of Basildon Town Centre”; the first shops opened in 1958.

name: Gloucester Park, Basildon
text: Your train passes near Gloucester Park, on the train's {side}, named after the Duke of Gloucester, who opened it in 1957. Basildon Sporting Village, on its northern edge, opened in 2011 and was first used as a training camp for the London Olympic Games of 2012.

name: Langdon Nature Reserve
text: Your train passes near Langdon Nature Reserve, on the train's {side}, 210 hectares of woodland, meadows and lakes run by the Essex Wildlife Trust. It covers the Dunton Plotlands, small plots lived on by smallholders and weekenders from the 1930s to the 1980s, and the remains of their little buildings can still be seen.

name: Church of St Laurence, Upminster
text: Your train passes near St Laurence's Church in Upminster, on the train's {side}, the minster that gave the place its name. Its 13th-century tower played a crucial part in the Reverend William Derham's first accurate measurement of the speed of sound.

name: Church of St Margaret, Bowers Gifford
text: Your train passes close to St Margaret's Church at Bowers Gifford, on the train's {side}, built by the Gifford family and dating from 1350. It once served a remote village among the estuary marshes, and its three bells were cast in 1380.

name: Hadleigh Castle
text: Your train passes near Hadleigh Castle, on the train's {side}, built after 1215 by Hubert de Burgh and later remodelled by Edward III. It stands on soft London clay, and subsidence and the sale of its stone in the 16th century have left it a ruin overlooking the Thames Estuary.

name: HMS Wilton (M1116)
text: Your train passes close to HMS Wilton, on the train's {side}, the first warship in the world built of glass-reinforced plastic, nicknamed “HMS Tupperware”. The Royal Navy retired the minehunter in 1994; after being sold in 2001 she became the home of the Essex Yacht Club at Leigh-on-Sea.

name: Palace Theatre, Westcliff-on-Sea
text: Your train passes near the Palace Theatre in Westcliff-on-Sea, on the train's {side}, opened in October 1912 and named the “Palace of Varieties” a month later. It closed in a money crisis in 1969, but a petition by the Palace Theatre Club saw it reopen in 1970.

name: Cliffs Pavilion
text: Your train passes near the Cliffs Pavilion, on the train's {side}, the largest purpose-built arts venue in Essex. Building began in 1939 but stopped for the war, and the site lay empty as “Southend's white elephant” until work restarted in 1963; Sir Bernard Miles opened the theatre in July 1964.

name: Southend Cliff Railway
text: Your train passes near the Southend Cliff Railway, on the train's {side}, a little lift between the clifftop and the beach that first ran on a bank holiday in August 1912. It stands on the site of a moving walkway of 1901, a forerunner of the escalator.

name: Southchurch Hall
text: Your train passes near Southchurch Hall, on the train's {side}, a moated medieval house built between about 1321 and 1364. Farming families lived there until the 1920s; it was restored and given to the town in 1930, and its Great Hall still looks much as it did in the 14th century.

name: Danish Camp, Shoeburyness
text: Your train passes near the Danish Camp, on the train's {side}, the remains of a defended prehistoric settlement whose ramparts are thought to have been about 40 feet wide and 12 feet high. The Viking leader Hastein built a camp at Shoebury in about 894.

name: St Mary's Church, Watford
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Watford's parish church, on the train's {side}, whose oldest parts date from around 1230. During repairs in 1871 the basin of a 12th-century font was found built into the walls of the tower.

name: St Matthew's Church, Oxhey
text: Your train passes close to St Matthew's Church in Oxhey, on the train's {side}, built in 1880 in red brick, with touches of early Art Nouveau. Its Lady Chapel has bright stained glass from about 1916 by Karl Parsons.

name: Colchester Castle
text: Your train passes near Colchester Castle, on the train's {side}, whose Norman keep is the largest of its kind anywhere in Europe. It is so big because it was built on the base of the Roman Temple of Claudius, and it has housed Colchester's museum since 1860.

name: Willis Building, Ipswich
text: Your train passes near the Willis Building in Ipswich, on the train's {side}, an office block clad in dark glass, designed by Norman Foster and Wendy Cheesman and built between 1970 and 1975. In 1991 it became the newest building in Britain to be listed Grade I.

name: Torr Vale Mill
text: Your train passes near Torr Vale Mill, on the train's {side}, a cotton mill at the bottom of the Torrs gorge, built in the late 1780s and first powered by two waterwheels. It made towelling until December 2000, the longest unbroken run of cotton production in the UK.

name: Bugsworth Basin
text: Your train passes near Bugsworth Basin, on the train's {side}, at the end of the Peak Forest Canal, once a busy meeting point with the Peak Forest Tramway for limestone and burnt lime. Volunteers restored it from 1968, and it reopened to boats at Easter 1999.

name: Cowburn Tunnel
text: Your train goes through Cowburn Tunnel, 3,702 yards long and the deepest railway tunnel in England, at 875 feet. It was dug from both ends, and the two halves met on July 18th 1891.

name: Church of the Holy and Undivided Trinity, Edale
text: Your train passes near Edale's Church of the Holy and Undivided Trinity, on the train's {side}, built in 1885 and 1886 to replace a chapel of 1633 across the road. Its tower, finished in 1889, rises 88 feet.

name: Navio Roman Fort
text: Your train passes near the site of Navio Roman fort, on the train's {side}, above a tight bend of the River Noe. A list of the world's places from about 700 AD records it, with roads to Buxton, to the fort near Glossop and to Manchester.

name: St Michael and All Angels' Church, Hathersage
text: Your train passes near Hathersage's parish church, on the train's {side}, which dates from the 14th century. Stones in its churchyard mark what is claimed to be the grave of Robin Hood's companion Little John.

name: Padley Gorge
text: Your train passes close to Padley Gorge, on the train's {side}, a deep, narrow wooded valley that is one of the furthest inland examples of temperate rainforest in the UK. Its stream, Burbage Brook, used to form the boundary between Derbyshire and Yorkshire.

name: Dinting Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Dinting Viaduct, also known as Dinting Arches, over Glossop Brook and the Manchester to Sheffield road. It opened in 1844 on the original Woodhead line, and seven brick piers were added to strengthen it from 1918 to 1920.

name: Hadfield
text: Your train passes the town of Hadfield, on the train's {side}, which stood in for the fictional Royston Vasey in the BBC comedy The League of Gentlemen.

name: North Road, Glossop
text: Your train passes close to North Road, on the train's {side}, a cricket ground that was home to Glossop North End during their years in the Football League. Their first league match there, on September 3rd 1898, was a win over Blackburn Rovers by four goals to one, in front of 4,000 people.

name: Torrs Hydro
text: Your train passes near Torrs Hydro, on the train's {side}, a community-owned hydroelectric scheme on the River Goyt in New Mills. Its 11-tonne screw turbine, 2.4 metres across, has made electricity since 2008; the £100,000 to build it was raised from 200 members.

name: Transhipment Warehouse, Whaley Bridge
text: Your train passes close to the Transhipment Warehouse at Whaley Bridge, on the train's {side}, built in 1801 across the head of the Peak Forest Canal and extended after the railway arrived in 1832. Goods and minerals were moved there to and from the many working boats serving local industry.

name: Combs Reservoir
text: Your train passes Combs Reservoir, on the train's {side}, built in 1797 as the first reservoir to feed the Peak Forest Canal. The railway runs alongside its western shore.

name: The Bull Ring, Dove Holes
text: Your train passes near the Bull Ring, on the train's {side}, a Neolithic henge with a burial mound beside it, evidence that people lived at Dove Holes in the late Stone Age.

name: Buxton Crescent
text: Your train passes near the Crescent in Buxton, on the train's {side}, designed by John Carr of York for the fifth Duke of Devonshire and built between 1780 and 1789. It was reopened in 2020 as a hotel and spa, facing St Ann's Well, where warm spring water has flowed for thousands of years.
